_readme: Triaged dependency advisories. Read by scripts/check-advisories.mjs — run it with
`pnpm audit:ci`. Nothing runs it for you: this repository has no CI, so the discipline
this file encodes is only as good as the habit of running the command.
An entry here is NOT 'ignore this'. It is a dated, signed statement that the advisory
cannot reach anything we ship, plus a deadline for looking again. The gate fails if an
entry expires while the advisory is still present, and it also fails if an entry stops
matching anything — so once a dependency is upgraded, the entry MUST be deleted. That is
what stops this file from turning into the permanent mute that every ignore-list becomes.
id       GHSA identifier, exactly as reported by `pnpm audit --json`
module   the package the advisory is against; cross-checked, so a copied id cannot
silently keep covering a different package
severity informational, for reading this file without running the audit
reason   at least 40 characters saying why it is not exploitable HERE and what the
plan is. Not 'transitive' — say what reaches it and what does not.
url      the advisory, so the next person can re-read it rather than trust this line
expires  YYYY-MM-DD, at most 183 days out (scripts/check-advisories.mjs MAX_TRIAGE_DAYS)
Only `high` and `critical` need an entry. Lower severities are printed by the gate on
every run and do not block — see the BLOCKING comment in the script for why.

advisories.reason: REAL AND FIXABLE — do not renew this entry. SQL injection via improperly escaped identifiers in the ORM that fronts every tenant-scoped query, so this is the one advisory in this file that reaches production code. It is listed only to keep the gate meaningful while the upgrade lands: `pnpm --filter @forge/db up drizzle-orm@0.45.2`, then run the tenancy suite (test:int) because the identifier-escaping change touches generated SQL. Short expiry on purpose.

Denial of service via an infinite loop in the ICNS parser, reached only through metro, the React Native bundler. It runs on a developer machine and in the `expo export` build step, never in a shipped artifact, and the only images it parses are the ones committed to this repo. No fix has been released for any version, so there is nothing to upgrade to; the exit is a metro bump when Expo ships one.

Same package, same path and same reasoning as GHSA-w3rx-r6r6-pgpr: infinite loops in the JXL and HEIF parsers inside metro's asset pipeline. Build-time only, inputs are our own committed assets, and no patched version exists. Tracked together with the ICNS advisory and cleared by the same metro upgrade.

A custom generator called with size zero loops forever. Reached through next -> postcss, which is the CSS build pipeline: it executes during `next build`, never at request time, and no code in this repo calls nanoid at all, let alone with an attacker-controlled size. postcss pins the vulnerable range transitively, so the fix arrives with a Next.js release rather than a direct bump.

Host confusion via skipped IDN canonicalisation. Reached only through @commitlint/cli -> ajv, which parses JSON Schema for commit-message linting: it runs on a developer's machine via the commit-msg hook and in the PR-title job, against our own commit titles. It is not a dependency of any application or of anything that reaches the runtime image. Cleared by an ajv release picking up fast-uri >= 3.1.6.

Server-side request forgery via malformed IPv6 normalisation, in the same commitlint -> ajv path as GHSA-5jgf-p345-68v8. Nothing in that path makes an outbound request, and the only input it ever sees is a commit message written by one of the two people with push access. Cleared by the same ajv upgrade.

Server-side request forgery via repeated hostname percent-decoding, same commitlint -> ajv path and same reasoning as the other two fast-uri entries: lint-time only, trusted input, no outbound request anywhere on the path. Grouped so all four clear together on one ajv upgrade.

Host confusion via percent-encoded scheme normalisation, the fourth advisory on the commitlint -> ajv path. Same containment: it is reached only while linting a commit message, never by the API, the web apps or the mobile apps, and never with untrusted input. Cleared by the same ajv upgrade as the other three.
